html:
The yearly trading season at Mocha, the main Red Sea port of Yemen in the 1600s, when ships from India and ships from Egypt met to swap goods.

The monsoon winds set the calendar. Ships from Gujarat and other Indian ports sailed in with cloth, rice and spices. From the north came a ship from Suez carrying silver coin and goods from Cairo. Merchants met at Mocha to trade and then sailed home on the turning winds. If either side arrived late, the season failed and the merchants waited a year.

Yemen's own export was coffee from its mountains. As coffee drinking spread through the Ottoman world and then Europe, Mocha became the world's coffee port and lent its name to a kind of coffee. The Dutch and English East India Companies opened offices there in the early 1600s.

The trade faded after coffee was planted elsewhere, first in Java and then the Caribbean, in the 1700s.
